patch.value: A promoted generation could store a padded or blank approval identity, consuming none of the budget it was promoted under

The approved promotion budget is counted by comparing each promoted generation's stored approval to the approval item id with strict equality. The parse boundary trimmed parent but not approval, and accepted an empty approval because it is non-null and so satisfies the promotion-evidence invariant. A generation body carrying an approval of two spaces, or of the approval id with surrounding whitespace, was therefore promoted while matching no approval id and consuming none of that approval's budget.

value.text: Reported by CodeRabbit on unbraind/pm-rl#12 as a Major data-integrity finding, and reproduced before it was applied: parseGenerationSpec trimmed parent at the parse boundary but stored approval verbatim, while countPromotedUnderApproval compares the stored approval to the approval id by strict equality. A hand-authored Generation body is all that is needed; the promote command never has to be called with a padded flag.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Fixed at the parse boundary rather than at the comparison, and a blank approval is refused as empty_approval rather than normalized to null. Normalizing a blank to null would silently downgrade a promoted record to one missing its evidence, so the promotion-evidence invariant would then report a different defect than the one present. The promote command also trims its approval flag so the id it looks up and the identity it stores are the same string.

value.text: An identity that is compared by strict equality must be normalized where it is parsed, not where it is compared, and every such field must be normalized together. This defect existed only because a previous round trimmed parent and stopped there: the same file, the same parse function, the same failure mode, one field later. When a normalization bug is fixed, enumerate every stored identity in the record and fix the class.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: A blank value that is non-null passes any invariant written as a null check. The promotion-evidence invariant asks whether approval is non-null, so an empty string satisfied it while matching no approval id - the record was simultaneously promoted-with-evidence and promoted-under-nothing. Presence checks on identity fields must test for a usable identity, not for the absence of null.

value.text: Review round seven produced five findings. Four were applied. One was refused with evidence: the claim that a padded --parent reaches storage is false, because stringOption returns value.trim() and maps a blank to undefined, so the value is already normalized before the register command sees it. The proposed fix would have restated a normalization the boundary already performs. Kept as an end-to-end guard on the option boundary instead, verified by removing the trim from stringOption and confirming the test fails.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: The same evidence corrects something I asserted in the previous round and CodeRabbit stored as a learning: I said trimming --approval was needed because normalizing only the parse side would leave --approval with surrounding whitespace failing a lookup it should satisfy. That was wrong. stringOption had already trimmed it, so the flag-side trim was redundant from the start and has been removed. The parse-boundary normalization is the one that matters, because a generation body can be hand-authored without ever passing through the flag.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: An absent parent key was refused as invalid_parent with a message stating parent must be a string or null - for a seed body whose absent parent IS null. Every other optional field in the parser already collapsed undefined to null before validating; parent was the last that did not. Fixed, with the non-seed case still refused but now for the reason true of it (missing_parent) rather than for a type it never violated.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Both refusals were withdrawn by the reviewer with explicit reasoning. On the parent trim it accepted that stringOption normalizes before the command sees the value, and accepted the correction that the same applies to approvalId - stating that the meaningful normalization is in parseGenerationSpec because persisted specifications bypass command-option processing. On the history edit it accepted that comment_edit is an appended hash-bound correction event that does not rewrite the earlier comment_add, and said it had applied an existing pm-history learning too broadly. Recording this because a refusal that is accepted is only worth the evidence attached to it: both were reproduced or read off the actual file before being argued.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: The fastest way to test a review finding is to write the test it implies and watch what happens. A finding that is true produces a failing test; a finding that is false produces a passing one, which is indistinguishable from a vacuous test unless you already know which you are looking at. Both cases here were resolved that way in minutes, and one of them exposed an error in my own previous round that had already been stored as a reviewer learning.

value.text: Round nine, ten findings, all applied. Two were code and both were real. A cyclic parent chain made buildAncestry return a TRUNCATED ancestry with no error, and on the strict path findContaminationPath then compares only the generations the walk reached, so an environment reachable only past the repeat point is never compared and a contaminated candidate passes a gate that reported nothing wrong. It now refuses as lineage_cycle on the strict path and stays tolerant for the view. Separately revertPromotingWrite restored a body captured BEFORE the lock, so a peer edit landing between that read and the lock would be silently discarded on a failed close; it now restores the in-lock re-read.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: The tolerant arm of the cycle guard was caught by the coverage gate rather than by review: neither member of a two-node cycle is a head, since each is the other's parent, so head enumeration never walks into the loop and the non-strict break was unreachable from the test as first written. A third generation hanging off the cycle makes it a head and reaches the path. Worth recording because the gate found a genuinely unexercised branch rather than a formality.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: The remaining eight findings were all current-state records or docs that had outlived what they describe: this item's own file notes still claimed a flag trim removed a round earlier, pm-rl-32a9 still called the invalidation frontier invisible after shipping the view that renders it, pm-rl-81oc's acceptance criteria and expected result omitted the registered-seed exception, pm-rl-6fb5's resolution predated three changes its own completion note records, the README wrote rl lineage where the command is pm rl lineage and documented only the named-head mode, one test hardcoded a tracker id, and the same-generation race test demanded every loser report already promoted when a bounded lock wait can legitimately report lock_conflict instead.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Round ten, six findings, all applied. The Major one was the other half of a defect I fixed a round earlier and thought was complete: the revert path had been corrected to use the in-lock body, but the promoting write on the SUCCESS path still rendered from the pre-lock spec, so a peer edit that does not set promoted passed the already-promoted guard and was then overwritten with no receipt. Fixing it properly needed more than swapping the source: promoting from the in-lock spec alone would record a contamination and gap verdict computed from provenance the record no longer has, so the fields that decision consumed are now compared under the lock and a change refuses as generation_changed_under_lock, while an edit to any other field survives the write.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: That guard also made an earlier test unreachable, which is worth recording as a pattern. The revert test injected its peer edit into base_checkpoint, a field the promotion decision consumes, so the new guard refused before the failing close and the revert path was never exercised - the test failed for the right reason. Retargeting the peer edit to training_config restored what it was written to check. A new refusal can silently hollow out an existing test by making its scenario unreachable, and the only signal is that the test starts failing for a reason unrelated to its name.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Round eleven, eight findings, all applied. The two Major ones were the same gap from opposite sides: my in-lock guard compared only the candidate's own fields, while the contamination verdict is computed by walking every ancestor and reading each one's environment version, and the README I wrote the round before claimed the broader guarantee. A peer editing an ANCESTOR leaves the leaf byte-identical and the verdict stale. Fixed by re-deciding contamination inside the lock over a fresh ancestry walk, which subsumes the leaf comparison entirely since the candidate is the walk's first entry, and by narrowing the README to what the code enforces.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: The test for that fix took four attempts and every intermediate version was vacuous. Version one injected the peer edit on the candidate read, which lands before the pre-lock walk, so the pre-lock check caught it and the test passed with the fix removed. Version two moved the trigger to the approval read, which is correctly between the two walks, but the assertion still matched provenance-unreadable messages, so any failure satisfied it. Version three tightened the assertion and still passed, because the fixture used the candidate's own environment as the held-out evaluation context, making the candidate contaminated from the start. Only version four - a second registered environment that nothing references until the peer edit points the seed at it - fails against the reverted implementation. Each intermediate version looked correct and asserted something true.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: A concurrency test has two independent ways to be vacuous and both look like a passing test: the injection can fire at the wrong point in the sequence, and the fixture can already satisfy the condition before injection. Checking the assertion text is not enough; the only reliable check is running it against the reverted implementation, and when it still passes, finding out which of the two causes it was rather than tightening the assertion and trying again.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Round twelve, four findings, all applied. The Major one was the FOURTH instance in this pull request of one pattern: a value read before the writer lock and consumed by a decision inside it. The approval's permitted count was parsed pre-lock and compared against an in-lock count, so an approval narrowed while a caller waited would be compared against the capacity it had before, and the promotion would exceed the approval that governs it. The budget is a comparison between two values and only one of them was being re-read.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Rather than fix the fourth instance alone, I enumerated every pre-lock value the in-lock apply consumes and classified each. Stale and now fixed: the approval spec. Already re-read: the generation body, the generation spec, the contamination ancestry, the promoted count. Not a concurrency hazard: proxy score, held-out score, gap and evidence, which come from the caller's own scores file and flags rather than from the tracker, so no peer can change them mid-invocation. The audit is what closes the pattern; fixing instances one per round is what kept it open.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: A mutual-exclusion lock only protects the values re-read inside it. Every value computed before the lock and consumed by a decision inside it is stale by construction, and each one is a separate defect that presents identically. When the first is found, enumerate all of them at once and classify each as re-read, invariant for the invocation, or stale - because they are indistinguishable from correct code until the exact interleaving occurs, and a reviewer will find them one per round otherwise.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Round thirteen, nine findings, all applied. Two matter beyond their size. First, the pre-lock audit I called complete last round had missed a site: budget_permitted in the returned details still read the pre-lock approval spec, so the value was re-read for the DECISION and not for the RECEIPT. An audit that enumerates decision inputs and stops there misses the outputs that report them. Second, the identity-normalization class had two members I never enumerated, because I had only ever looked at parsed specification fields: collection_runs entries inside the JSON fence, and the environment identity on a collection Run item.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: The Major security finding on the Run environment turned out not to be reachable, and establishing that was worth more than the fix. A Run whose toon file literally stores environment with surrounding spaces reads back trimmed through the SDK, verified twice with different padded values, so a padded run identity never reaches the strict-equality contamination compare. The trim stays anyway as defence in depth, because this feeds a security gate and the normalization it relies on lives in another package - and the dependency is now pinned by a test asserting the SDK boundary trims, so if that ever changes pm-rl finds out from its own suite rather than from a contaminated promotion passing. collection_runs is the opposite case and the asymmetry is the useful part: the JSON fence is opaque body text pm does not normalize, so padding there IS reachable and is trimmed at the parse boundary.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: affected_version on a Generation was computed over the whole specification at registration, so promotion - which legitimately rewrites promoted, approval, both scores, gap and promotion evidence - left the recorded identity disagreeing with the stored body. Nothing consumes that rule for Generations today, but verifyEnvironmentIdentity applies exactly it to Environments, so any later integrity check would have reported every promoted generation as mutated. Resolved by choosing the contract rather than patching the symptom: the hash covers the provenance subset only, so the identity pins what a generation was trained FROM, survives promotion, and stays checkable by re-hashing the stored body.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: An audit is only as complete as the question it asks. Enumerating every pre-lock value consumed by an in-lock DECISION missed the one consumed by the in-lock RECEIPT, and enumerating every identity in a parsed specification missed the identities that arrive as pm item fields and as entries inside the JSON fence. Both times the enumeration was carried out faithfully and the frame was too narrow, which is indistinguishable from completeness until someone asks the wider question.
